transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in today?

Well, doc... I came in because I just keep having these thoughts lately that my family might be better off if I didn't wake up. It got so heavy it actually scared me enough to tell my supervisor. Which isn't like me, you know? Usually, me and him just talk about the floor operations. Like Tuesday, we had this absolute mess on the loading dock. The new kid they hired to drive the forklift completely jammed a pallet of parts sideways against the bay doors. I've been telling upper management for months, you can't just throw these young guys on the floor without proper training, it's a huge liability. You gotta show them the ropes first or somebody's gonna get hurt. But... what was I saying? Right, yeah, the thoughts. They just kind of spooked me, so I blurted it out to him, and he told me I needed to come see someone.
Have you been feeling down or depressed most days lately?

I don't know if I'd say most days... honestly, it's hard to even keep track of the days right now. I get into the warehouse around 4:30 in the morning just to check the overnight manifests, so they all kind of blur together. And let me tell you, the shipping delays lately are just brutal. We had a rig coming down from Michigan last week that sat at a weigh station for two whole days because of some completely ridiculous paperwork mix-up. Two days! And of course, the client is calling my cell, chewing my ear off about their inventory like I personally control the Department of Transportation. I told the guy, look, buddy, I just manage the floor, I don't drive the trucks. People just have no patience anymore, everybody wants everything yesterday and they don't care what it takes to get it done. 

But... wait, what were you asking me? About feeling down? I mean, I guess I'm not really sure how often it is. I haven't really been keeping a tally or anything. I just know it got heavy enough to scare me the other day.
Did something stressful happen in your life around the time these thoughts started?

Well, yeah, actually. This whole change in me... it's been going on for about two weeks now. Right around the time my daughter left Georgia for the military. She joined the Army, you know? Just packed up and shipped out to basic. Which, I mean, I'm proud of her, don't get me wrong. But the military these days... it's not like when my uncle served. He was in the Navy back in the seventies, stationed out in San Diego. Used to tell me these crazy stories about the mess hall and how they'd get away with murder on shore leave. He actually brought me back this real nice Zippo lighter once, had the ship's crest engraved right on the front. Wish I knew what happened to that thing. I think I might have lost it when we moved out of the old house on Elm Street. That house had the worst plumbing, let me tell you. Every time it rained hard, the basement would flood. I spent half my weekends down there with a shop vac just trying to keep the drywall from rotting out. 

But, uh... yeah. Two weeks. Ever since she left, I've just been... off.
Are you thinking about killing yourself?

Well, I... I wouldn't say I'm sitting there making a plan or nothing. It's more just... like I said before, those thoughts about how maybe everybody would just be better off if I didn't wake up in the morning. That's what spooked me enough to say something to my boss. I mean, usually I keep things pretty close to the chest, you know? Like my dad always said, you don't air your dirty laundry. He was a tough old bird, my dad. Worked at the steel mill for thirty-five years, never took a sick day. Even when he broke his thumb with a hammer, he just taped it up with electrical tape and went right back to the line. They don't make guys like that anymore. Now you got guys calling out because their allergies are acting up. Allergies! I tell you, the work ethic in this country is just going straight down the tubes. 

But, uh... yeah. I'm not looking to hurt myself, doc. It's just those thoughts about not waking up. That's why I'm here.
Since your daughter left, have you been feeling sad most of the day?

Sad? I mean... I guess I wouldn't call it sad, exactly. And I don't know about most of the day. It's just this... weight, you know? Like when you're trying to move a pallet jack that's got a busted wheel. 

Speaking of which, I've been fighting with corporate for three months to get us new jacks. Three months! They keep sending me these emails with all these fancy spreadsheets attached, talking about budget allocations and quarters. I can barely even read the damn things on my computer screen. I told them, look, I don't need a spreadsheet, I need equipment that actually rolls. You got guys out on the floor throwing their shoulders out trying to pull a ton of dog food across the concrete. Dog food is the absolute worst to load, by the way. Those paper bags tear if you even look at them wrong, and then you got kibble spilling all over the place, which just brings in the mice. We had an exterminator come out... oh, man, must've been back in the spring. Guy charged the company an arm and a leg, and I swear to you he just sprayed tap water around the baseboards. Total scam artist. 

But... I'm sorry, doc, my mind is wandering again. What did you ask me? About being sad? Yeah, I don't really know if it's all day long or what. I just know I haven't been feeling right since she shipped out.
Since your daughter left, have you lost interest in things you usually enjoy?

Well, yeah, I suppose so. I used to do a lot of stuff around the house. Like, I'd always be out back messing with my tomato plants. Got these Big Boys, you know? But the dirt around here is basically just pure red clay. You gotta mix in so much peat moss and compost just to get a single root to take. My neighbor, Gary, he swears by dumping eggshells and old coffee grounds in the dirt, but I keep telling him he's just setting up a buffet for the raccoons. And man, those raccoons are getting bold. Tore up my trash cans last Tuesday. Had chicken bones and junk scattered all over the driveway. Took me an hour to hose it down, and the darn hose nozzle was leaking the whole time. It's that cheap plastic junk they sell down at the big box stores now. Used to be they made those things out of solid brass, right? You'd buy one and it would last you twenty years. Now you're lucky if the thing makes it through a single July without cracking in the sun. They just don't care about quality control anymore, everything's made as cheap as possible... 

But, uh... what was I saying? Oh, right. Things I enjoy. Yeah, I haven't even gone out to look at the garden. Same with my workbench down in the garage. Usually I'd be down there sanding some wood, or on Sundays I'd be watching the Falcons, or staying after church just talking with folks. But lately... I don't know. I just look at all that stuff—the bench, the plants, the games—and it's like it belongs to somebody else. I just don't have it in me to care about any of it right now.
Have you been waking up much earlier than usual and unable to get back to sleep?

Sleep? Nah, not really waking up early. If anything, it's just hard to get out of bed at all. But waking up at the crack of dawn? No. 

Though, speaking of mornings, you wouldn't believe the traffic on I-285 lately. Used to be you could leave the house at 6:00 AM and cruise right into the warehouse district, no problem. Now? Forget about it. They've been doing construction on that one overpass for, what, two years now? Two years to fix a bridge! And they always have those orange barrels blocking off the right lane for miles, but you never actually see anybody working. Just a bunch of guys in hard hats standing around drinking coffee. I swear, the city must be paying them by the hour to just lean on their shovels. And then you get these hotshot kids in their sports cars trying to zip around everybody and merge at the very last second. Almost took my bumper off last Thursday. I drive a '98 F-150, doc, solid steel. If that kid had hit me, his little plastic car would've folded up like an accordion. Best truck I ever owned, though the transmission's been slipping a little in second gear. My buddy Earl says he can rebuild it for me, but Earl's been saying he'll fix my lawnmower since last Thanksgiving, so I ain't holding my breath on that one. 

But, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, waking up early. Yeah, no, I haven't had that problem. I'm usually just laying there wishing I didn't have to get up.
For the past two weeks, have you been feeling this heavy way nearly every day?

Yeah, every single day. It's been like this for about two weeks now, right around the time my daughter shipped out of Georgia for the military. 

Man, Fort Benning... well, Fort Moore now, I guess they changed the name. But she went down there, and I told her, I said, "You better get used to the heat, kiddo, because South Georgia in the summer is like walking on the surface of the sun." I remember when I was down near Columbus for a distribution conference back in '09. We were supposed to be looking at these new automated conveyor systems, but the AC in the expo hall completely crapped out on the first day. Had a couple thousand guys in suits sweating through their shirts. They tried bringing in these giant industrial fans, but all that did was blow hot, humid air around like a giant hair dryer. And the catering! Don't even get me started on the catering. They served us this lukewarm chicken salad that had been sitting out, and half the management team from the Atlanta branch spent the next two days fighting over the bathrooms at the Holiday Inn. I stuck to the crackers and ginger ale, thank God. You gotta be careful with mayonnaise-based stuff when the temperature gets above eighty degrees, everybody knows that. It's just common sense. But these corporate event planners, they don't think about logistics, they just look at the price per head...

Wait, sorry doc. I'm doing it again, aren't I? You asked about how long I've been feeling heavy. Yeah, it's been every day for the last two weeks, ever since she left.
Over the past two weeks, have you been having trouble concentrating?

Yeah, concentration's been... it's been real tough. At the distribution center, I'll be sitting there staring at the schedule or the routing sheet, and my mind just won't lock in. You know? It's like I'm looking at the words, but they aren't meaning anything. And then I get these little staffing calls, guys calling out sick or whatever, and it feels like this massive problem I gotta solve, way bigger than it ought to be. 

Usually I can handle that stuff in my sleep. I mean, staffing a warehouse ain't rocket science, but you gotta know your people. Like Tommy on the loading dock, you can't put him with Martinez because they'll just argue about college football the whole shift. Martinez is a die-hard Bulldogs fan, right? Got the bumper sticker, the hat, probably got a bulldog tattooed on his backside for all I know. And Tommy, he went to Auburn for like a semester back in the nineties before he dropped out, but he still acts like he's on the coaching staff. They get into it over the dumbest things. Last year, Martinez actually threw a roll of packing tape at Tommy's head because of some call a referee made in a game that happened five years ago. I had to write them both up. HR wanted me to send them to some conflict resolution seminar downtown, but I told them, "Look, you put these two in a room with a whiteboard and a therapist, and somebody's gonna end up going through a window." Corporate HR, they don't get the warehouse culture. They think everybody communicates with "I feel" statements. If I walked onto the floor and started talking about my feelings, they'd laugh me right out of the building. You gotta talk to these guys on their level, you know? Firm, but fair. 

But, uh... yeah. Staring at the schedule. My brain's just in a fog lately. Can't focus on it at all.
Before these last two weeks, have you ever had another period like this in your life?

Well, looking back on it... yeah, I guess these low stretches have been coming around for about a year or so. But this one, right after my daughter shipped out, this one's hit me the absolute hardest. 

It's funny how things hit you, you know? Like when my old dog, Buster, passed away back in... must've been '18. He was a good boy, a lab mix. Found him wandering around the loading dock one morning, shivering, covered in grease. I took him home, cleaned him up with some Dawn dish soap—best thing for grease, by the way, cuts right through it. Anyway, Buster used to wait for me by the front door every single day. When he died, the house just felt... empty. Quiet. My wife, God rest her soul, she used to say that silence was golden, but I don't know about that. Sometimes silence is just loud. Like when the power goes out at the warehouse and the hum of the conveyors stops, and suddenly you can hear every little creak and groan of the metal roof. We had a blackout during that ice storm a few years back, and I had to stay overnight with a skeleton crew to make sure the pipes didn't freeze. We sat around in the breakroom with flashlights, eating stale vending machine pretzels and telling ghost stories. Old man Jenkins swore he saw a shadow moving in Aisle 4, but I told him it was just the raccoons that get in through the loading bays. Those things are smart, doc. I watched one figure out how to open a latch on a dumpster once. Just popped it right open like he had thumbs. 

But, uh, yeah. About a year I've been getting these spells. This one's just... it's a lot heavier.
Before this current stretch, did you ever have another period lasting at least two weeks when you felt this same heavy way nearly every day?

Yeah, like I was saying, it's... it's been about a year or so that these low stretches have been coming around. They'd last a couple weeks, maybe a little longer, where I'd just feel that same heaviness every day. But this one right now, after my daughter shipped out, this is the hardest it's ever hit me. 

It's strange how time works, though, isn't it? A year sounds like a long time, but it goes by in a blink. I remember when I first started at the warehouse, I thought I'd be there for maybe six months, just until I found something better. That was thirty years ago! Thirty years. I've seen guys come and go, seen the whole industry change. We used to do everything on paper, carbon copies. You had to press so hard with your pen your hand would cramp up by noon. Now it's all barcodes and scanners and computers that tell you exactly where everything is. Supposed to make it easier, but half the time the system goes down and nobody knows what to do because they don't know how to read a manifest anymore. I had a kid last week, couldn't have been more than nineteen, staring at a pallet of auto parts like it was an alien spaceship just because his scanner battery died. I told him, "Son, before you were born, we moved twice as much freight with half the technology." But they don't teach them how to think on their feet anymore. It's all just following the beep. 

But yeah, anyway... to answer your question, doc, I've had periods like this for about a year, but nothing quite this heavy.
Between these low stretches over the past year, did you ever get completely back to feeling like your usual self?

Well, that's the thing, isn't it? Back to my usual self... I'm not really sure I know what that means anymore. I mean, between those heavy spells, I guess I felt... different? But not exactly like the old me. 

You know, the old me used to rebuild carburetors on the weekend. Just for fun! Me and my buddy Sal, we'd get a twelve-pack of Miller Lite and just tear into an engine block in his garage. Sal had this incredible setup, pegboards covering every wall, every wrench outlined in black marker so you knew exactly where it went. He was a stickler for organization, Sal was. Worked as a machinist for Boeing for twenty years before he retired. He used to say, "A place for everything, and everything in its place." We rebuilt a '69 Mustang once, cherry red. Took us three years. We had to source the original parts from all over the country. Found a guy in New Mexico who had a pristine original steering wheel just sitting in a barn. Can you believe that? A barn! Covered in dust and chicken feathers, but underneath it was perfect. We drove out there in Sal's pickup, straight through, taking turns at the wheel. Ate nothing but beef jerky and gas station hot dogs the whole way. I tell you, my stomach wasn't right for a week after that, but man, the open road... there's nothing like it. Just the hum of the tires and the radio playing classic rock. 

But, uh... what were we talking about? Oh, right. Feeling normal. Yeah, I don't know if I ever really got back to normal between those low times. It's hard to say.
For the past two years, have you felt down or heavy more days than not?

Two years? Uh... well, I don't know about two whole years. Like I said, it's been about a year or so with these spells, but before that... I don't really think I felt heavy most days. Two years ago... man, two years ago was when I finally broke down and bought that John Deere riding mower. 

My knees were just giving out pushing that old Toro around the yard. Best investment I ever made, doc. It has that zero-turn radius, you know? You can spin on a dime right around the big oak tree in the front yard. And a cup holder! You wouldn't think a cup holder on a lawnmower is a big deal, but let me tell you, on a hot July afternoon with an ice-cold sweet tea... it is heaven. My neighbor Gary, he has this little electric push mower. Sounds exactly like a giant hair dryer. And he leaves his grass clippings right on the sidewalk. Drives me absolutely crazy. I always tell him he needs to sweep that up before it washes into the storm drain, but he just looks at me like I am speaking Greek. 

People these days just do not take pride in their property. You drive down my street, and half the houses have gutters overflowing with pine needles. I clean mine out twice a year, regular as clockwork. I even got a special attachment for the hose. It blasts the muck right out of there. You have to be careful on the ladder, though. One of the guys at the warehouse, Tommy, fell off a ladder last spring and shattered his collarbone. Just a freak accident, but he was out of work for months. We had to shuffle the whole shift schedule around to cover his loading dock. 

But, uh... wait, I lost my train of thought. What were you asking me? Something about two years?
Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually energized or wired for several days in a row, much more than your normal self?

Wired? Yeah, actually... there was a stretch a while back where I had just so much energy I didn't know what to do with it. I was waking up way before daylight. I mean, pitch black outside, the birds aren't even up yet, and I'm wide awake at the kitchen table, drawing up all these big plans for changes at the warehouse. Figured out a whole new way to route the forklifts. Then I'd be out in the freezing cold cleaning the garage, just jumping from one job to the next without even wanting to stop. 

While I was out there in the garage, I actually found my original Craftsman socket set. Buried under a tarp behind the snowblower. Let me tell you, they do not make tools like that anymore. Now it's all cheap metal from overseas that strips out the second you put any real torque on it. But this old Craftsman set, it's heavy. You can feel the quality in your hand. My dad bought me that set when I got my first truck, an '82 Chevy C10. Two-tone blue and silver. God, I loved that truck. The heater core blew out the second winter I had it, and I had to drive to work wrapped in a wool blanket for three months because I couldn't afford the parts to fix it. I finally got it patched up just in time for summer. Isn't that how it always goes? 

I ended up selling it to a guy a few towns over, and I still kick myself for it. I saw it parked outside a diner maybe five years later, and the guy had painted it this awful matte black. Looked like a chalkboard on wheels. It's a crime what some people do to classic vehicles. Just absolutely no respect for the original engineering. 

But, uh... yeah. I was just going and going, jumping from project to project. Didn't want to stop for a second.
During that energized stretch, did you need much less sleep than usual and still feel rested?

Sleep? Yeah, I guess so. I mean, like I said, I was up before the sun even thought about rising. Four hours, maybe five, and I was just ready to go. Didn't feel tired at all, honestly. Just... boom, eyes open, mind racing. 

It's funny you mention sleep, though, because normally I'm a solid eight-hour guy. Have to be, right? But my wife, she's a terrible sleeper. Always has been. She bought this weighted blanket last Christmas because she saw it on one of those morning shows. Thing weighs like twenty pounds. I tried it once and felt like I was being buried alive. I don't know how she stands it. She says it makes her feel secure, but to me, it's just a trap. If there's a fire in the middle of the night, you're going to spend five minutes just trying to wrestle your way out from under that thing. 

We actually had a small fire in the kitchen a few years back. The toaster oven shorted out. Scared the living daylights out of me. I had to use the extinguisher we kept under the sink, the one with the dry chemical stuff. Man, that powder gets absolutely everywhere. It took us weeks to clean it out of the grout on the backsplash. We ended up having to hire a professional cleaning crew because my wife's asthma started acting up from all the dust. The guy who came out to do the cleaning, Hector, he was a real character. Told us he used to be a rodeo clown down in Texas before he moved up here. Can you imagine that? Staring down a two-ton bull for a living. Takes a special kind of crazy, if you ask me. 

But, uh... wait. What were we talking about? Oh, the sleep thing. Yeah, I didn't need much sleep at all during that stretch. Just felt totally rested and ready to tackle the day.
During that energized stretch, did it cause serious problems at work, at home, or with other people?

Problems? Yeah, I guess you could say that. At home, I just completely let things go. Bills and responsibilities just piled up on the kitchen counter instead of me handling them like I normally would. I'm usually a stickler for getting the water bill paid the day it comes in. 

Speaking of the mail, our regular mailman, Dave, retired last month. Guy walked that route for twenty-five years. Calves the size of bowling balls. Now we have this new kid, can't be older than twenty, and he keeps putting our neighbor's mail in our box. I mean, the numbers are right there on the side of the house in brass. Four-inch brass numbers I bought at the hardware store. I had to drill right into the brick to mount them. Broke two masonry bits doing it, too. Brick is funny like that, you hit a hard spot and it just snaps the bit right off. You have to keep the drill perfectly straight or you're just asking for trouble. 

But anyway, yeah, the bills just sat there. And at work, it got pretty messy, too. I was going so fast that my mistakes got really serious. It got bad enough that one of the supervisors actually found me sitting out in my truck before dawn one morning and ended up getting occupational health involved. 

I was parked out under this big halogen light by the loading docks. I always park there to keep the catalytic converter thieves away. You know they can saw one of those off in under two minutes? Happened to my brother-in-law's car right in his own driveway. Just zip with a battery-powered Sawzall and they're gone into the night. Costs two grand to replace, and the insurance companies fight you tooth and nail on it. Anyway, they sent this occupational health lady down with a clipboard and everything to talk to me. She had these reading glasses on a little beaded chain around her neck. Reminded me exactly of my middle school librarian, Mrs. Gable. Mrs. Gable used to catch me trying to sneak out of study hall to go to the auto shop... 

Wait, I'm rambling again. Did that answer what you were asking about the problems?
During that energized stretch, did you ever hear or see things other people couldn’t, or believe something others said wasn’t true?

Hear or see things? No, no, nothing like that. I wasn't seeing ghosts or anything. My mind was just going a mile a minute, you know? 

Speaking of seeing things, though, you wouldn't believe the deer we've had in the yard lately. Huge bucks, right up by the back patio. My wife planted these hostas last spring, spent a fortune on them at that nursery out on Route 9. The one with the big fiberglass cow on the roof? They've had that cow up there since I was a kid. Anyway, the deer treat those hostas like a salad bar. Just munch them right down to the dirt. I tried putting up some of that netting, the black plastic stuff, but it's a real pain to work with. Gets tangled on every little branch and twig. I ended up wrapping it around my own ankle and nearly took a header into the birdbath. 

That birdbath is solid concrete, too. Weighs a ton. Had to use a hand truck to get it from the driveway to the backyard when we bought it. The wheels on the hand truck were a little low on air, and one of them popped right off the rim when I hit a root. Sounded like a gunshot. The neighbor's dog started barking, this little terrier mix that never shuts up... 

But, uh, no. No seeing things or hearing voices or anything crazy like that. Just the energy.
About how many days in a row did that energized stretch last?

How many days? Hmm, I'm not really sure, to be honest. I didn't exactly have a calendar out marking it down. 

Speaking of calendars, did you know they stopped giving those out at the auto parts store? Used to be, every December, you'd go in for a couple quarts of oil and they'd hand you one of those big glossy calendars with the classic cars on them. I had a whole collection going in the garage. 1969 Mustangs, '57 Chevys, you name it. Now? Nothing. They say it's all digital now, everybody just uses their phones. But you can't hang a phone on a pegboard above your workbench, can you? 

I spent all last weekend trying to organize that workbench. It's a disaster area. I've got coffee cans full of screws and nails that I've been saving since the Clinton administration. You never know when you're going to need a two-inch wood screw, right? But the problem is, I don't label the cans. So I spend twenty minutes dumping out Folgers cans just looking for one specific washer. My wife bought me one of those plastic organizer bins with the little drawers, but I don't trust the plastic. Seems flimsy. Drop a hammer on that thing and it'll shatter into a million pieces. 

I actually did drop a hammer on my toe once. A framing hammer, the heavy kind with the waffle face on the head. Right on the big toe. Turned purple instantly. I had to drill a hole in the nail with a tiny drill bit just to relieve the pressure... 

Wait, what were we talking about? The days? Yeah, I really couldn't tell you an exact number. It just sort of all blurred together while I was going so fast.
Did that energized stretch last a full week or longer?

A full week? I don't know, maybe? Like I said, I wasn't really keeping track of time. 

Time is a funny thing, though, isn't it? My grandfather used to have this grandfather clock in his hallway. Beautiful piece of woodwork, mahogany, I think. Or maybe cherry. Anyway, he had to wind it every single Sunday with this brass key. If he forgot, the whole thing would just stop dead on Tuesday afternoon. I remember being fascinated by the pendulum swinging back and forth. Tick, tock, tick, tock. 

He actually taught me how to tell time on that clock. None of this digital stuff they teach kids today. You had to know where the big hand and the little hand were. He gave me his old pocket watch when I turned twelve. An Elgin, silver case, real heavy in your hand. I carried it everywhere until I dropped it in a puddle down by the creek. The crystal smashed, water got inside, ruined the whole mechanism. Took it to a watchmaker downtown, guy named Mr. Henderson. He had this little magnifying glass squeezed into his eye, looked like a cyborg or something. He took one look at it and shook his head. Said it would cost more to fix than it was worth. 

I still have it, though, sitting in a drawer somewhere in the bedroom. Next to my old high school class ring. The stone fell out of that ring years ago. It was supposed to be a ruby, but I'm pretty sure it was just red glass. You know how those things are, they charge you an arm and a leg for a piece of cheap metal...

But yeah, a week? Longer? I really couldn't say for sure. It just felt like one long, fast stretch.
During that high-energy stretch, did you feel unusually good or on top of the world?

Yeah, I guess you could say that. Before this whole low spell hit, I was feeling way too fired up. Like everything was finally going my way, you know? Or, well, either that or I was snapping at folks over small things I'd normally just let slide. 

Speaking of snapping, my neighbor's dog—that little terrier mix I mentioned?—it snapped at the mail carrier last week. Just lunged right at his ankle while he was trying to put the mail in the box. The mail carrier is this younger guy, always wears those shorts, even when it's freezing out. I don't know how he does it. My knees ache if the temperature drops below fifty. I tried wearing those copper compression sleeves they sell on TV, the ones with the retired quarterback doing the commercial? Total waste of money. Might as well have wrapped my knees in tin foil. 

Anyway, the mail guy had to use his bag as a shield. The dog didn't break the skin, but the neighbor still had to come out and apologize. Brought the mail guy a gift card to the coffee shop down the street. That coffee shop used to be a hardware store when I was growing up. Old man Miller ran it. You could walk in there and buy a single nail if you wanted to. Try doing that at one of these big box stores today. They make you buy a box of five hundred, and they're all made of cheap pot metal that bends as soon as you hit it with a hammer. 

I was building a birdhouse a few years back and went through half a box of those cheap nails just trying to get the roof attached. Finally gave up and used wood glue. Gorilla glue, actually. That stuff expands like crazy. I got some on my thumb and it took me a week to peel it off. Felt like I was shedding my skin like a snake...

But, uh, yeah. Feeling good, feeling fired up, or just getting irritated real easy. That's how it was.

doctor.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
doctor.question: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in today?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I keep having these thoughts that my family might be better off if I didn't wake up, and that scared me enough to tell my supervisor.
target_item.reason: First turn of consultation, returning chief complaint.

patient.answer: Well, doc... I came in because I just keep having these thoughts lately that my family might be better off if I didn't wake up. It got so heavy it actually scared me enough to tell my supervisor. Which isn't like me, you know? Usually, me and him just talk about the floor operations. Like Tuesday, we had this absolute mess on the loading dock. The new kid they hired to drive the forklift completely jammed a pallet of parts sideways against the bay doors. I've been telling upper management for months, you can't just throw these young guys on the floor without proper training, it's a huge liability. You gotta show them the ropes first or somebody's gonna get hurt. But... what was I saying? Right, yeah, the thoughts. They just kind of spooked me, so I blurted it out to him, and he told me I needed to come see someone.

inference.note: Initial differential based on suicidal ideation with unclear duration and depressive symptoms: includes depressive episode, recurrent depressive disorder, adjustment disorder, and unspecified anxiety disorder. Tangentiality/inattention noted but insufficient on first turn to add or confirm another diagnosis.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the suicidal thoughts are part of a major depressive episode by assessing depressed mood, which best distinguishes depression from adjustment disorder or unspecified anxiety at this point.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling down or depressed most days lately?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about depressed mood, but my symptom profile does not include a specific symptom for depressed mood (only related symptoms like Loss of Interest, Worthlessness/Guilt, etc.). Therefore, there is no direct match for depressed mood.

patient.answer:
I don't know if I'd say most days... honestly, it's hard to even keep track of the days right now. I get into the warehouse around 4:30 in the morning just to check the overnight manifests, so they all kind of blur together. And let me tell you, the shipping delays lately are just brutal. We had a rig coming down from Michigan last week that sat at a weigh station for two whole days because of some completely ridiculous paperwork mix-up. Two days! And of course, the client is calling my cell, chewing my ear off about their inventory like I personally control the Department of Transportation. I told the guy, look, buddy, I just manage the floor, I don't drive the trucks. People just have no patience anymore, everybody wants everything yesterday and they don't care what it takes to get it done. 

But... wait, what were you asking me? About feeling down? I mean, I guess I'm not really sure how often it is. I haven't really been keeping a tally or anything. I just know it got heavy enough to scare me the other day.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a clear recent stressor temporally linked to the suicidal thoughts, which would help distinguish adjustment disorder from a primary depressive or anxiety disorder.
doctor.question: Did something stressful happen in your life around the time these thoughts started?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This whole change in me has been going on for about two weeks since my daughter left Georgia for the military.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about any stressful events around the time the thoughts started, which relates to the onset and duration of the current episode (my daughter leaving for the military two weeks ago).

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, actually. This whole change in me... it's been going on for about two weeks now. Right around the time my daughter left Georgia for the military. She joined the Army, you know? Just packed up and shipped out to basic. Which, I mean, I'm proud of her, don't get me wrong. But the military these days... it's not like when my uncle served. He was in the Navy back in the seventies, stationed out in San Diego. Used to tell me these crazy stories about the mess hall and how they'd get away with murder on shore leave. He actually brought me back this real nice Zippo lighter once, had the ship's crest engraved right on the front. Wish I knew what happened to that thing. I think I might have lost it when we moved out of the old house on Elm Street. That house had the worst plumbing, let me tell you. Every time it rained hard, the basement would flood. I spent half my weekends down there with a shop vac just trying to keep the drywall from rotting out. 

But, uh... yeah. Two weeks. Ever since she left, I've just been... off.

inference.note: F43.2 moves to the top because symptoms began about 2 weeks ago in clear temporal relation to a psychosocial stressor (daughter leaving for military). Depressive disorders remain possible given passive suicidal thoughts, but duration and syndrome are not yet established. F41.9 remains a broader fallback.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the suicidal thoughts include intent to act, to assess immediate safety and help distinguish a major depressive episode from a stress reaction or nonspecific anxiety.
doctor.question: Are you thinking about killing yourself?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I keep having these thoughts that my family might be better off if I didn't wake up, and that scared me enough to tell my supervisor.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about suicidal thoughts, which matches the Death_Suicide symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, I... I wouldn't say I'm sitting there making a plan or nothing. It's more just... like I said before, those thoughts about how maybe everybody would just be better off if I didn't wake up in the morning. That's what spooked me enough to say something to my boss. I mean, usually I keep things pretty close to the chest, you know? Like my dad always said, you don't air your dirty laundry. He was a tough old bird, my dad. Worked at the steel mill for thirty-five years, never took a sick day. Even when he broke his thumb with a hammer, he just taped it up with electrical tape and went right back to the line. They don't make guys like that anymore. Now you got guys calling out because their allergies are acting up. Allergies! I tell you, the work ethic in this country is just going straight down the tubes. 

But, uh... yeah. I'm not looking to hurt myself, doc. It's just those thoughts about not waking up. That's why I'm here.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms are tied to a bereavement/adjustment trigger versus a broader depressive episode by assessing persistent low mood since the daughter left.
doctor.question: Since your daughter left, have you been feeling sad most of the day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about depressed or sad mood, but there is no specific symptom for depressed mood in the provided symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Sad? I mean... I guess I wouldn't call it sad, exactly. And I don't know about most of the day. It's just this... weight, you know? Like when you're trying to move a pallet jack that's got a busted wheel. 

Speaking of which, I've been fighting with corporate for three months to get us new jacks. Three months! They keep sending me these emails with all these fancy spreadsheets attached, talking about budget allocations and quarters. I can barely even read the damn things on my computer screen. I told them, look, I don't need a spreadsheet, I need equipment that actually rolls. You got guys out on the floor throwing their shoulders out trying to pull a ton of dog food across the concrete. Dog food is the absolute worst to load, by the way. Those paper bags tear if you even look at them wrong, and then you got kibble spilling all over the place, which just brings in the mice. We had an exterminator come out... oh, man, must've been back in the spring. Guy charged the company an arm and a leg, and I swear to you he just sprayed tap water around the baseboards. Total scam artist. 

But... I'm sorry, doc, my mind is wandering again. What did you ask me? About being sad? Yeah, I don't really know if it's all day long or what. I just know I haven't been feeling right since she shipped out.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is loss of interest or pleasure, which helps distinguish a major depressive episode from an adjustment disorder or nonspecific anxiety.
doctor.question: Since your daughter left, have you lost interest in things you usually enjoy?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I used to mess with my tomato plants, sand wood at my bench, watch the Falcons, and stay after church talking, but lately I just look at all that like it belongs to somebody else.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks about losing interest in usually enjoyed activities, which corresponds to the Loss of Interest symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, I suppose so. I used to do a lot of stuff around the house. Like, I'd always be out back messing with my tomato plants. Got these Big Boys, you know? But the dirt around here is basically just pure red clay. You gotta mix in so much peat moss and compost just to get a single root to take. My neighbor, Gary, he swears by dumping eggshells and old coffee grounds in the dirt, but I keep telling him he's just setting up a buffet for the raccoons. And man, those raccoons are getting bold. Tore up my trash cans last Tuesday. Had chicken bones and junk scattered all over the driveway. Took me an hour to hose it down, and the darn hose nozzle was leaking the whole time. It's that cheap plastic junk they sell down at the big box stores now. Used to be they made those things out of solid brass, right? You'd buy one and it would last you twenty years. Now you're lucky if the thing makes it through a single July without cracking in the sun. They just don't care about quality control anymore, everything's made as cheap as possible... 

But, uh... what was I saying? Oh, right. Things I enjoy. Yeah, I haven't even gone out to look at the garden. Same with my workbench down in the garage. Usually I'd be down there sanding some wood, or on Sundays I'd be watching the Falcons, or staying after church just talking with folks. But lately... I don't know. I just look at all that stuff—the bench, the plants, the games—and it's like it belongs to somebody else. I just don't have it in me to care about any of it right now.

doctor.intent: Determine whether he has a core neurovegetative symptom of major depression to distinguish MDD from adjustment disorder/anxiety.
doctor.question: Have you been waking up much earlier than usual and unable to get back to sleep?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about early morning awakening/insomnia, which is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Sleep? Nah, not really waking up early. If anything, it's just hard to get out of bed at all. But waking up at the crack of dawn? No. 

Though, speaking of mornings, you wouldn't believe the traffic on I-285 lately. Used to be you could leave the house at 6:00 AM and cruise right into the warehouse district, no problem. Now? Forget about it. They've been doing construction on that one overpass for, what, two years now? Two years to fix a bridge! And they always have those orange barrels blocking off the right lane for miles, but you never actually see anybody working. Just a bunch of guys in hard hats standing around drinking coffee. I swear, the city must be paying them by the hour to just lean on their shovels. And then you get these hotshot kids in their sports cars trying to zip around everybody and merge at the very last second. Almost took my bumper off last Thursday. I drive a '98 F-150, doc, solid steel. If that kid had hit me, his little plastic car would've folded up like an accordion. Best truck I ever owned, though the transmission's been slipping a little in second gear. My buddy Earl says he can rebuild it for me, but Earl's been saying he'll fix my lawnmower since last Thanksgiving, so I ain't holding my breath on that one. 

But, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, waking up early. Yeah, no, I haven't had that problem. I'm usually just laying there wishing I didn't have to get up.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive symptoms are occurring nearly every day, which helps distinguish a major depressive episode from an adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: For the past two weeks, have you been feeling this heavy way nearly every day?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This whole change in me has been going on for about two weeks since my daughter left Georgia for the military.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the specific timeframe of the current symptoms, which corresponds to the two-week duration of the current depressive episode.

patient.answer:
Yeah, every single day. It's been like this for about two weeks now, right around the time my daughter shipped out of Georgia for the military. 

Man, Fort Benning... well, Fort Moore now, I guess they changed the name. But she went down there, and I told her, I said, "You better get used to the heat, kiddo, because South Georgia in the summer is like walking on the surface of the sun." I remember when I was down near Columbus for a distribution conference back in '09. We were supposed to be looking at these new automated conveyor systems, but the AC in the expo hall completely crapped out on the first day. Had a couple thousand guys in suits sweating through their shirts. They tried bringing in these giant industrial fans, but all that did was blow hot, humid air around like a giant hair dryer. And the catering! Don't even get me started on the catering. They served us this lukewarm chicken salad that had been sitting out, and half the management team from the Atlanta branch spent the next two days fighting over the bathrooms at the Holiday Inn. I stuck to the crackers and ginger ale, thank God. You gotta be careful with mayonnaise-based stuff when the temperature gets above eighty degrees, everybody knows that. It's just common sense. But these corporate event planners, they don't think about logistics, they just look at the price per head...

Wait, sorry doc. I'm doing it again, aren't I? You asked about how long I've been feeling heavy. Yeah, it's been every day for the last two weeks, ever since she left.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has impaired concentration/indecisiveness as another core symptom of a major depressive episode, helping distinguish major depression from adjustment disorder or unspecified anxiety.
doctor.question: Over the past two weeks, have you been having trouble concentrating?

target_item.name: Diminished_Thinking
target_item.manifestation: At the distribution center I stare at the schedule or the routing sheet and my mind just won't lock in, so little staffing calls feel bigger than they ought to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about trouble concentrating, which matches the Diminished_Thinking symptom.

patient.answer:
Yeah, concentration's been... it's been real tough. At the distribution center, I'll be sitting there staring at the schedule or the routing sheet, and my mind just won't lock in. You know? It's like I'm looking at the words, but they aren't meaning anything. And then I get these little staffing calls, guys calling out sick or whatever, and it feels like this massive problem I gotta solve, way bigger than it ought to be. 

Usually I can handle that stuff in my sleep. I mean, staffing a warehouse ain't rocket science, but you gotta know your people. Like Tommy on the loading dock, you can't put him with Martinez because they'll just argue about college football the whole shift. Martinez is a die-hard Bulldogs fan, right? Got the bumper sticker, the hat, probably got a bulldog tattooed on his backside for all I know. And Tommy, he went to Auburn for like a semester back in the nineties before he dropped out, but he still acts like he's on the coaching staff. They get into it over the dumbest things. Last year, Martinez actually threw a roll of packing tape at Tommy's head because of some call a referee made in a game that happened five years ago. I had to write them both up. HR wanted me to send them to some conflict resolution seminar downtown, but I told them, "Look, you put these two in a room with a whiteboard and a therapist, and somebody's gonna end up going through a window." Corporate HR, they don't get the warehouse culture. They think everybody communicates with "I feel" statements. If I walked onto the floor and started talking about my feelings, they'd laugh me right out of the building. You gotta talk to these guys on their level, you know? Firm, but fair. 

But, uh... yeah. Staring at the schedule. My brain's just in a fog lately. Can't focus on it at all.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has a history of prior depressive episodes to distinguish a single major depressive episode from recurrent depression or an adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: Before these last two weeks, have you ever had another period like this in your life?

target_item.name: Depressive Episode Duration
target_item.manifestation: Looking back, the low stretches have been coming around for about a year, but this one after my daughter left has hit me the hardest.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I have had previous periods of feeling like this, which corresponds to the duration/history of my depressive episodes.

patient.answer:
Well, looking back on it... yeah, I guess these low stretches have been coming around for about a year or so. But this one, right after my daughter shipped out, this one's hit me the absolute hardest. 

It's funny how things hit you, you know? Like when my old dog, Buster, passed away back in... must've been '18. He was a good boy, a lab mix. Found him wandering around the loading dock one morning, shivering, covered in grease. I took him home, cleaned him up with some Dawn dish soap—best thing for grease, by the way, cuts right through it. Anyway, Buster used to wait for me by the front door every single day. When he died, the house just felt... empty. Quiet. My wife, God rest her soul, she used to say that silence was golden, but I don't know about that. Sometimes silence is just loud. Like when the power goes out at the warehouse and the hum of the conveyors stops, and suddenly you can hear every little creak and groan of the metal roof. We had a blackout during that ice storm a few years back, and I had to stay overnight with a skeleton crew to make sure the pipes didn't freeze. We sat around in the breakroom with flashlights, eating stale vending machine pretzels and telling ghost stories. Old man Jenkins swore he saw a shadow moving in Aisle 4, but I told him it was just the raccoons that get in through the loading bays. Those things are smart, doc. I watched one figure out how to open a latch on a dumpster once. Just popped it right open like he had thumbs. 

But, uh, yeah. About a year I've been getting these spells. This one's just... it's a lot heavier.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has had a prior depressive episode lasting at least two weeks, which would distinguish recurrent major depressive disorder from a single depressive episode or adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: Before this current stretch, did you ever have another period lasting at least two weeks when you felt this same heavy way nearly every day?

target_item.name: Depressive Episode Duration
target_item.manifestation: Looking back, the low stretches have been coming around for about a year, but this one after my daughter left has hit me the hardest.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking to clarify the duration of previous depressive episodes, specifically if they lasted at least two weeks, which relates to the history and duration of the patient's depressive episodes over the past year.

patient.answer:
Yeah, like I was saying, it's... it's been about a year or so that these low stretches have been coming around. They'd last a couple weeks, maybe a little longer, where I'd just feel that same heaviness every day. But this one right now, after my daughter shipped out, this is the hardest it's ever hit me. 

It's strange how time works, though, isn't it? A year sounds like a long time, but it goes by in a blink. I remember when I first started at the warehouse, I thought I'd be there for maybe six months, just until I found something better. That was thirty years ago! Thirty years. I've seen guys come and go, seen the whole industry change. We used to do everything on paper, carbon copies. You had to press so hard with your pen your hand would cramp up by noon. Now it's all barcodes and scanners and computers that tell you exactly where everything is. Supposed to make it easier, but half the time the system goes down and nobody knows what to do because they don't know how to read a manifest anymore. I had a kid last week, couldn't have been more than nineteen, staring at a pallet of auto parts like it was an alien spaceship just because his scanner battery died. I told him, "Son, before you were born, we moved twice as much freight with half the technology." But they don't teach them how to think on their feet anymore. It's all just following the beep. 

But yeah, anyway... to answer your question, doc, I've had periods like this for about a year, but nothing quite this heavy.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the prior depressive periods were separated by full remission, which would distinguish recurrent major depressive disorder from a single prolonged episode or adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: Between these low stretches over the past year, did you ever get completely back to feeling like your usual self?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about inter-episode recovery or returning to a euthymic baseline between depressive episodes, which is not specifically covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, that's the thing, isn't it? Back to my usual self... I'm not really sure I know what that means anymore. I mean, between those heavy spells, I guess I felt... different? But not exactly like the old me. 

You know, the old me used to rebuild carburetors on the weekend. Just for fun! Me and my buddy Sal, we'd get a twelve-pack of Miller Lite and just tear into an engine block in his garage. Sal had this incredible setup, pegboards covering every wall, every wrench outlined in black marker so you knew exactly where it went. He was a stickler for organization, Sal was. Worked as a machinist for Boeing for twenty years before he retired. He used to say, "A place for everything, and everything in its place." We rebuilt a '69 Mustang once, cherry red. Took us three years. We had to source the original parts from all over the country. Found a guy in New Mexico who had a pristine original steering wheel just sitting in a barn. Can you believe that? A barn! Covered in dust and chicken feathers, but underneath it was perfect. We drove out there in Sal's pickup, straight through, taking turns at the wheel. Ate nothing but beef jerky and gas station hot dogs the whole way. I tell you, my stomach wasn't right for a week after that, but man, the open road... there's nothing like it. Just the hum of the tires and the radio playing classic rock. 

But, uh... what were we talking about? Oh, right. Feeling normal. Yeah, I don't know if I ever really got back to normal between those low times. It's hard to say.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient has had a persistently depressed mood for at least two years, which would help distinguish recurrent major depressive episodes from persistent depressive disorder and clarify whether this is more than an adjustment reaction.
doctor.question: For the past two years, have you felt down or heavy more days than not?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling down more days than not for the past two years (criteria for Persistent Depressive Disorder/Dysthymia), which is not covered by any specific item in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Two years? Uh... well, I don't know about two whole years. Like I said, it's been about a year or so with these spells, but before that... I don't really think I felt heavy most days. Two years ago... man, two years ago was when I finally broke down and bought that John Deere riding mower. 

My knees were just giving out pushing that old Toro around the yard. Best investment I ever made, doc. It has that zero-turn radius, you know? You can spin on a dime right around the big oak tree in the front yard. And a cup holder! You wouldn't think a cup holder on a lawnmower is a big deal, but let me tell you, on a hot July afternoon with an ice-cold sweet tea... it is heaven. My neighbor Gary, he has this little electric push mower. Sounds exactly like a giant hair dryer. And he leaves his grass clippings right on the sidewalk. Drives me absolutely crazy. I always tell him he needs to sweep that up before it washes into the storm drain, but he just looks at me like I am speaking Greek. 

People these days just do not take pride in their property. You drive down my street, and half the houses have gutters overflowing with pine needles. I clean mine out twice a year, regular as clockwork. I even got a special attachment for the hose. It blasts the muck right out of there. You have to be careful on the ladder, though. One of the guys at the warehouse, Tommy, fell off a ladder last spring and shattered his collarbone. Just a freak accident, but he was out of work for months. We had to shuffle the whole shift schedule around to cover his loading dock. 

But, uh... wait, I lost my train of thought. What were you asking me? Something about two years?

doctor.intent: Assess for any history of manic or hypomanic episodes to rule out bipolar disorder as an explanation for the recurrent depressive episodes.
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually energized or wired for several days in a row, much more than your normal self?

target_item.name: Increased_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I had so much energy for a while that I was up before daylight planning warehouse changes, cleaning the garage, and jumping from one job to the next without wanting to stop.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about periods of feeling 'unusually energized or wired,' which maps to abnormally increased energy or activity.

patient.answer:
Wired? Yeah, actually... there was a stretch a while back where I had just so much energy I didn't know what to do with it. I was waking up way before daylight. I mean, pitch black outside, the birds aren't even up yet, and I'm wide awake at the kitchen table, drawing up all these big plans for changes at the warehouse. Figured out a whole new way to route the forklifts. Then I'd be out in the freezing cold cleaning the garage, just jumping from one job to the next without even wanting to stop. 

While I was out there in the garage, I actually found my original Craftsman socket set. Buried under a tarp behind the snowblower. Let me tell you, they do not make tools like that anymore. Now it's all cheap metal from overseas that strips out the second you put any real torque on it. But this old Craftsman set, it's heavy. You can feel the quality in your hand. My dad bought me that set when I got my first truck, an '82 Chevy C10. Two-tone blue and silver. God, I loved that truck. The heater core blew out the second winter I had it, and I had to drive to work wrapped in a wool blanket for three months because I couldn't afford the parts to fix it. I finally got it patched up just in time for summer. Isn't that how it always goes? 

I ended up selling it to a guy a few towns over, and I still kick myself for it. I saw it parked outside a diner maybe five years later, and the guy had painted it this awful matte black. Looked like a chalkboard on wheels. It's a crime what some people do to classic vehicles. Just absolutely no respect for the original engineering. 

But, uh... yeah. I was just going and going, jumping from project to project. Didn't want to stop for a second.

inference.note: Added F31.9 because the newly endorsed period of markedly increased energy with decreased need for sleep/early waking and increased goal-directed activity raises concern for bipolar spectrum disorder; F41.9 is less supported and dropped.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the energized period included decreased need for sleep, a key discriminator for bipolar disorder versus recurrent unipolar depression or adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: During that energized stretch, did you need much less sleep than usual and still feel rested?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a decreased need for sleep, which is a specific symptom of mania/hypomania. This symptom is not included in the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Sleep? Yeah, I guess so. I mean, like I said, I was up before the sun even thought about rising. Four hours, maybe five, and I was just ready to go. Didn't feel tired at all, honestly. Just... boom, eyes open, mind racing. 

It's funny you mention sleep, though, because normally I'm a solid eight-hour guy. Have to be, right? But my wife, she's a terrible sleeper. Always has been. She bought this weighted blanket last Christmas because she saw it on one of those morning shows. Thing weighs like twenty pounds. I tried it once and felt like I was being buried alive. I don't know how she stands it. She says it makes her feel secure, but to me, it's just a trap. If there's a fire in the middle of the night, you're going to spend five minutes just trying to wrestle your way out from under that thing. 

We actually had a small fire in the kitchen a few years back. The toaster oven shorted out. Scared the living daylights out of me. I had to use the extinguisher we kept under the sink, the one with the dry chemical stuff. Man, that powder gets absolutely everywhere. It took us weeks to clean it out of the grout on the backsplash. We ended up having to hire a professional cleaning crew because my wife's asthma started acting up from all the dust. The guy who came out to do the cleaning, Hector, he was a real character. Told us he used to be a rodeo clown down in Texas before he moved up here. Can you imagine that? Staring down a two-ton bull for a living. Takes a special kind of crazy, if you ask me. 

But, uh... wait. What were we talking about? Oh, the sleep thing. Yeah, I didn't need much sleep at all during that stretch. Just felt totally rested and ready to tackle the day.

inference.note: Added evidence for a bipolar spectrum disorder: distinct prior period of increased energy with decreased need for sleep and racing mind suggests hypomanic/manic symptoms, making F31.9 more likely. Recurrent depressive episodes remain possible; current episode still temporally related to daughter's departure, so F43.2 not fully ruled out yet.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the prior energized period caused functional impairment consistent with mania rather than milder hypomania, helping distinguish bipolar disorder from recurrent or single-episode depression/adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: During that energized stretch, did it cause serious problems at work, at home, or with other people?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: At work, my mistakes got serious enough that a supervisor found me sitting in my truck before dawn and got occupational health involved. At home, I’ve let bills and responsibilities pile up instead of handling them like I normally would.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the energized (hypomanic) period caused serious problems at work, home, or socially, which corresponds to the functional impairment criterion.

patient.answer:
Problems? Yeah, I guess you could say that. At home, I just completely let things go. Bills and responsibilities just piled up on the kitchen counter instead of me handling them like I normally would. I'm usually a stickler for getting the water bill paid the day it comes in. 

Speaking of the mail, our regular mailman, Dave, retired last month. Guy walked that route for twenty-five years. Calves the size of bowling balls. Now we have this new kid, can't be older than twenty, and he keeps putting our neighbor's mail in our box. I mean, the numbers are right there on the side of the house in brass. Four-inch brass numbers I bought at the hardware store. I had to drill right into the brick to mount them. Broke two masonry bits doing it, too. Brick is funny like that, you hit a hard spot and it just snaps the bit right off. You have to keep the drill perfectly straight or you're just asking for trouble. 

But anyway, yeah, the bills just sat there. And at work, it got pretty messy, too. I was going so fast that my mistakes got really serious. It got bad enough that one of the supervisors actually found me sitting out in my truck before dawn one morning and ended up getting occupational health involved. 

I was parked out under this big halogen light by the loading docks. I always park there to keep the catalytic converter thieves away. You know they can saw one of those off in under two minutes? Happened to my brother-in-law's car right in his own driveway. Just zip with a battery-powered Sawzall and they're gone into the night. Costs two grand to replace, and the insurance companies fight you tooth and nail on it. Anyway, they sent this occupational health lady down with a clipboard and everything to talk to me. She had these reading glasses on a little beaded chain around her neck. Reminded me exactly of my middle school librarian, Mrs. Gable. Mrs. Gable used to catch me trying to sneak out of study hall to go to the auto shop... 

Wait, I'm rambling again. Did that answer what you were asking about the problems?

doctor.intent: Differentiate bipolar I disorder from bipolar II disorder or recurrent/unipolar depression by determining whether the prior energized episode included psychotic symptoms, which would strongly support a manic episode and bipolar I.
doctor.question: During that energized stretch, did you ever hear or see things other people couldn’t, or believe something others said wasn’t true?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychotic symptoms (hallucinations or delusions), which are not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Hear or see things? No, no, nothing like that. I wasn't seeing ghosts or anything. My mind was just going a mile a minute, you know? 

Speaking of seeing things, though, you wouldn't believe the deer we've had in the yard lately. Huge bucks, right up by the back patio. My wife planted these hostas last spring, spent a fortune on them at that nursery out on Route 9. The one with the big fiberglass cow on the roof? They've had that cow up there since I was a kid. Anyway, the deer treat those hostas like a salad bar. Just munch them right down to the dirt. I tried putting up some of that netting, the black plastic stuff, but it's a real pain to work with. Gets tangled on every little branch and twig. I ended up wrapping it around my own ankle and nearly took a header into the birdbath. 

That birdbath is solid concrete, too. Weighs a ton. Had to use a hand truck to get it from the driveway to the backyard when we bought it. The wheels on the hand truck were a little low on air, and one of them popped right off the rim when I hit a root. Sounded like a gunshot. The neighbor's dog started barking, this little terrier mix that never shuts up... 

But, uh, no. No seeing things or hearing voices or anything crazy like that. Just the energy.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the past energized episode lasted long enough to distinguish mania/hypomania from a depressive disorder or adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: About how many days in a row did that energized stretch last?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of the energized (hypomanic) stretch, which is not covered by the 'duration' key (that refers to the current depressive episode) or any other item in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
How many days? Hmm, I'm not really sure, to be honest. I didn't exactly have a calendar out marking it down. 

Speaking of calendars, did you know they stopped giving those out at the auto parts store? Used to be, every December, you'd go in for a couple quarts of oil and they'd hand you one of those big glossy calendars with the classic cars on them. I had a whole collection going in the garage. 1969 Mustangs, '57 Chevys, you name it. Now? Nothing. They say it's all digital now, everybody just uses their phones. But you can't hang a phone on a pegboard above your workbench, can you? 

I spent all last weekend trying to organize that workbench. It's a disaster area. I've got coffee cans full of screws and nails that I've been saving since the Clinton administration. You never know when you're going to need a two-inch wood screw, right? But the problem is, I don't label the cans. So I spend twenty minutes dumping out Folgers cans just looking for one specific washer. My wife bought me one of those plastic organizer bins with the little drawers, but I don't trust the plastic. Seems flimsy. Drop a hammer on that thing and it'll shatter into a million pieces. 

I actually did drop a hammer on my toe once. A framing hammer, the heavy kind with the waffle face on the head. Right on the big toe. Turned purple instantly. I had to drill a hole in the nail with a tiny drill bit just to relieve the pressure... 

Wait, what were we talking about? The days? Yeah, I really couldn't tell you an exact number. It just sort of all blurred together while I was going so fast.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the past energized episode lasted at least 7 days, which best distinguishes bipolar I disorder from bipolar II disorder and recurrent/unipolar depression at this point.
doctor.question: Did that energized stretch last a full week or longer?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of the energized (hypomanic/manic) episode, which is not specified in the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
A full week? I don't know, maybe? Like I said, I wasn't really keeping track of time. 

Time is a funny thing, though, isn't it? My grandfather used to have this grandfather clock in his hallway. Beautiful piece of woodwork, mahogany, I think. Or maybe cherry. Anyway, he had to wind it every single Sunday with this brass key. If he forgot, the whole thing would just stop dead on Tuesday afternoon. I remember being fascinated by the pendulum swinging back and forth. Tick, tock, tick, tock. 

He actually taught me how to tell time on that clock. None of this digital stuff they teach kids today. You had to know where the big hand and the little hand were. He gave me his old pocket watch when I turned twelve. An Elgin, silver case, real heavy in your hand. I carried it everywhere until I dropped it in a puddle down by the creek. The crystal smashed, water got inside, ruined the whole mechanism. Took it to a watchmaker downtown, guy named Mr. Henderson. He had this little magnifying glass squeezed into his eye, looked like a cyborg or something. He took one look at it and shook his head. Said it would cost more to fix than it was worth. 

I still have it, though, sitting in a drawer somewhere in the bedroom. Next to my old high school class ring. The stone fell out of that ring years ago. It was supposed to be a ruby, but I'm pretty sure it was just red glass. You know how those things are, they charge you an arm and a leg for a piece of cheap metal...

But yeah, a week? Longer? I really couldn't say for sure. It just felt like one long, fast stretch.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the prior energized episode involved abnormally elevated or euphoric mood, which helps distinguish bipolar disorder from recurrent or stress-related unipolar depression when duration is unclear.
doctor.question: During that high-energy stretch, did you feel unusually good or on top of the world?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Before this low spell hit, I was either feeling way too fired up like everything was finally going my way or snapping at folks over small things I normally let slide.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question about feeling 'unusually good or on top of the world' directly probes for an abnormally elevated or expansive mood during the high-energy stretch.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I guess you could say that. Before this whole low spell hit, I was feeling way too fired up. Like everything was finally going my way, you know? Or, well, either that or I was snapping at folks over small things I'd normally just let slide. 

Speaking of snapping, my neighbor's dog—that little terrier mix I mentioned?—it snapped at the mail carrier last week. Just lunged right at his ankle while he was trying to put the mail in the box. The mail carrier is this younger guy, always wears those shorts, even when it's freezing out. I don't know how he does it. My knees ache if the temperature drops below fifty. I tried wearing those copper compression sleeves they sell on TV, the ones with the retired quarterback doing the commercial? Total waste of money. Might as well have wrapped my knees in tin foil. 

Anyway, the mail guy had to use his bag as a shield. The dog didn't break the skin, but the neighbor still had to come out and apologize. Brought the mail guy a gift card to the coffee shop down the street. That coffee shop used to be a hardware store when I was growing up. Old man Miller ran it. You could walk in there and buy a single nail if you wanted to. Try doing that at one of these big box stores today. They make you buy a box of five hundred, and they're all made of cheap pot metal that bends as soon as you hit it with a hammer. 

I was building a birdhouse a few years back and went through half a box of those cheap nails just trying to get the roof attached. Finally gave up and used wood glue. Gorilla glue, actually. That stuff expands like crazy. I got some on my thumb and it took me a week to peel it off. Felt like I was shedding my skin like a snake...

But, uh, yeah. Feeling good, feeling fired up, or just getting irritated real easy. That's how it was.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
opening_question.question: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient currently has a depressive episode with passive suicidal ideation, anhedonia, low energy/difficulty getting out of bed, and impaired concentration lasting about two weeks. Crucially, he also reports a prior distinct period of abnormally increased energy with decreased need for sleep, racing mind, increased goal-directed activity, elevated/irritable mood, and clear functional impairment severe enough for occupational health involvement. This history supports a bipolar spectrum disorder rather than unipolar depression or adjustment disorder. Psychotic symptoms were denied.
